text: tendencies, and emergence of the multiplex world order have made the US-India ties more important than ever. Since the 1990s, India and the US have been trying to get closer and build stronger partnerships. However, this relationship is not devoid of challenges. The US expects India to make clear choices in favour of the US-led coalition. It also expects India to cut off ties with Russia, Iran, and other so-called rogue states. For India, however, these are not just sovereign choices; these are based on hard-headed realistic assessments of the unfolding geopolitical scenario. To protect such decisions while bolstering cooperation with the US (and its allies), ‘strategic autonomy’ and ‘multi-alignment’ have been devised as India’s guiding principles. The decision to stick to Russian defence supplies is deeply embedded in India’s approach to having diversified sources of defence supplies, while Iran is one of the prime partners in the South West Asian region. With the rapidly unfolding situation in Afghanistan, Iran’s role for India has acquired greater salience. Indian policymakers are also careful not to give the impression that their policies are subservient to the US interests. The notion of strategic autonomy has not been pushed aside by Indian policymakers. Explaining India’s under - standing of strategic autonomy, the foreign secretary of India Harsh Vardhan Shringla ( 2020 ) in his address at the National Defence College in 2020 stated: The concept of “strategic autonomy” is a function of the prevalent structure of the interna - tional order making it a more relative concept as opposed to an absolute one. In today’s multipolar world, all countries are, at some point or the other, susceptible to external pressures . . . . As a result, the world around India changed fundamentally in the last few decades. It is also evident that the structural change that shaped the global order was predominantly a result of the shift in the economic balance of power. In addition, new and emerging issues threats from terrorism, cyber security, climate change, and pandemics called for India to adjust its policies to the new realities. Our strategic autonomy thus necessitated the association between an autonomous foreign policy and security decision- making capability and the preservation of material assets, both technical and economic. Shringla’s statement touches on the essence of India’s approach. A sovereign, independent, and rising non-western power cannot afford to remain oblivious to its strategic interests worldwide. India’s interests in Central Asia, the Persian Gulf, the Arab region, Latin America, Africa, Eurasia, and even in South Asia (Pakistan and Afghanistan) and Southeast Asia (Myanmar) may not necessarily be in sync with that of the US. Even with Vietnam, which has been lauded as one of the most promising US partners in the Indo-Pacific, India’s interests are not the same as those of the US. In Non Alignment 2.0 report, Khilnani et al. ( 2014 , p. 6) state: Strategic autonomy has been the defining value and continuous goal of India’s international policy ever since the inception of the Republic. Defined initially in the terminology of Non- Alignment, that value we believe continues to remain at the core of India’s global engage - ments even today, in a world that has changed drastically since the mid-20th century. Acolytes of the alliance system often tend to target India’s long-standing commitment to strategic autonomy as flawed and pretentious. Such assessments tend to overlook that for rising powers such as India, strategic autonomy functions as a tool to ensure survival and maximise leverage in any given situation To ward off such criticism and sufficiently explain India’s foreign policy approach, Dr. S. Jaishankar, the External Affairs Minister of India, officially pronounced India’s ‘multi-alignment’ policy. With strategic autonomy as one of THE ROUND TABLE 53

text: its tools, the multi-alignment policy aims to engage as many international stakeholders and partners as possible, based on India’s own politico-strategic and economic calculations. Highlighting the importance of multi-alignment in Indian foreign policy, Jaishankar states (Jaishankar, 2020 , p. 93): Taking off on non-alignment, it is sometimes useful to speak of multi-alignment. It appears more energetic and participative as compared to an earlier posture of abstention or non- involvement. He adds that multi-alignment facilitates a weaker player in soliciting or manipulating stronger forces to its own advantage (Jaishankar, 2020 , p. 62). Jaishankar’s reiteration of ‘multi-alignment’ in Indian foreign policy sums up the aspirations and strategic orienta - tions of a rising India. The critical importance of a deeper partnership with the US and its allies cannot be overstated. However, India is seemingly unwilling to compromise on its strategic autonomy in making foreign policy choices. This is witnessed in the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, where despite the Western criticism and pressure, India has not gone against Russia citing its dependence on Moscow for defence equipment and regional strategic considerations invol - ving China. Partnership with countries such as Iran and Russia is pivotal to India’s presence in their respective areas of strategic influence. It is Russia, after all, with which India has opened a direct and dedicated channel of communication – a hotline between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi – to deal with the situation post-US withdrawal from Afghanistan. Likewise, India’s long-standing partnership with Iran would help India effectively deal with its strategic vulnerabilities emanating out of the Taliban takeover of Afghanistan. Both these issues are critical in shaping India’s relations with the US. Sensing India’s growing ties with the US, Russia has also normalised ties with Pakistan, compelling India to pursue ‘multi-alignment’ in its foreign policy, which may be seen as a pro-active, action-oriented, and more forthcoming version of the non-alignment policy. Highlighting the key facets of multi-alignment in India’s foreign policy, Jaishankar states (Jaishankar, 2020 , pp. 16–17): For the near term, India has little choice but to pursue a mix of multiple approaches, some orthodox and others more imaginative. But in all of them, partnerships with global interests could make a significant difference. Much of that would revolve around the West and Russia. But China, now the world’s second-largest economy, can hardly be disregarded in any calculation. Leveraging them all may not be easy but still no less necessary for that. Mastering mind games and playing hardball are also musts in a more visceral world. To do all that, it is vital that we come to terms with its complex dynamics. Only then can India successfully execute strategic policies for a new era. Clearly, despite India’s attempts to inch closer to the West, its pursuit of multi-alignment is likely to continue along with some time-tested elements of non-alignment. As S.D. Muni also noted in one of his social media comments (Muni, 2022 ): Dr Jaishankar’s statement that India cannot be a “pale imitation” of others defines Modi foreign policy’s (Modi’s multi-alignment policy) Nehruvian moment. This is what ‘non- alignment’ and ‘strategic autonomy’ were all about. text: flops on Indo-Pacific projects demonstrate that more than its commitment, the US policy endurance will be scrutinised by its friends in the region. Small, middle and rising powers of the Indo-Pacific region are still uncertain about the sincerity and endurance of the US commitment to the region on military, diplomatic, and economic fronts under all circum - stances. These security anxieties have motivated ASEAN countries to practise hedging in their foreign policies. A sustainable commitment of the US is a major factor shaping their national priorities and policies, and justifiably so. India’s multi-alignment policy cannot be appreciated without embedding it in the historical context and realities therein. Conclusion India’s non-alignment policy during the Cold War years was based on both idealism and pragmatism. Aligned with normative principles, it helped India steer clear of bloc politics. During the Cold War period, India not only had to focus on nation-building but also had several pressing issues to deal with such as the border conflicts with China and Pakistan, turbulence in the Indian subcontinent, and concerns related to nuclear weapons. Times have changed and non-alignment (in its original form) is no longer the mainstay of contemporary Indian foreign policy. Considering that the systemic realities of international relations have changed, it seems logical to shed some of the notions of non-alignment attached to the Cold War times as well. With regard to non-alignment - a major development that has taken place is India’s greater insistence on ‘strategic autonomy’, and the pursuit of multi-alignment underthe Modi 2.0 government. The ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, widening rift between Russia and the West, and the US-China tensions – all these develop - ments underline creeping polarisation, though with distinct differences, in contemporary global politics. India’s (and even Indonesia’s) claims to play a peace role in Ukraine war and now efforts to articulate the voice of the global south fall into the non-alignment mode although with several notable changes. Considering the fluid nature of international relations and great power dynamics, India is looking for a sufficiently wide strategic window – elbow room of sorts to manoeuvre effectively in regional and international scenarios. It is this insistence on multi-alignment that gives India the wiggle room to keep its defence ties intact with Russia and strategic cooperation with Iran functional while inching closer to the US and its Asian allies via the Quad. The sudden withdrawal of the US troops from Afghanistan and its willingness to engage China again is a sure sign of the unpredict - ability of international politics. India seems cognisant of these developments and has tried to keep its multi-alignment policy intact as the mainstay of foreign policy formulation. India’s insistence on multi-alignment policy also serves as a fine tribute to some of its cherished normative principles of non-alignment, even as multi-alignment has brought in stronger elements of hard-headed and pragmatic notions of foreign policy-making.
